operational_definition.core: Primary or explicit secondary reanalysis of tested operational crowd interventions: controlling inflow, queueing, movement/route advice, leaders or intentionally placed flow-regulating obstacles; include real-event reconstruction of operational crowd-control failure. This is an operational adjudication definition, not a claim that the question excludes broader interventions.
operational_definition.boundary: Keep pandemic-distance policies, transport scheduling, facility geometry and more indirect behavioral/information manipulations for broader-scope sensitivity. Secondary reviews remain available as reported evidence but are not counted as new original campaigns.
operational_definition.exclude: No tested intervention-effect contrast under the operational definition, or auxiliary prediction/calibration/basic descriptive methods. Exclusion does not mean the entire source is irrelevant to crowd safety.
operational_definition.unit_policy: A publication is never automatically an independent study. Preserve empirical collection batches, computational intervention suites and virtual-human tasks as components within linked campaigns. Repeated trials, simulation parameter settings and videos are not new independent studies. Reanalyses inherit the original data family. Shared model/venue alone is not proof of duplicate computational results.

evidence.anchor_text: The data used in this study were ﬁrst published by Holl (2016 ). Data were collected on the 19th and 20th of June 2013 as part of a large experimental study on pedestrian dynamics conducted at the Düsseldorf trade fair centre (for details on all experiments and participant recruitment, see Holl (2016 )). Experiments on the ﬁrst and second day involved 319 and 603 participants, respectively.

A total of ﬁve runs across experimental condi- tions were excluded from our analysis. In these runs the inﬂow rate was controlled via hand signs introducing 1 s or 2 s intervals between pedestrians. This resulted in highly artiﬁcial dynamics that were not the interest of the study presented here.

Using white, opaque, 2.5 m high barriers, we marked an experimental arena that consisted of two 4.0 m wide and 14.0 m long corridors that intersected half-way along their length at right angles, creating a symmetric setup with a central crossing of 16 m 2 surface area (see Fig. 1 A).

Simulations are performed by sampling from the posterior distribution of models and parameters (obtained from ﬁtting models to the corresponding data). For each experiment shown, we run 10 0 0 simulations, starting with the initial condition of no pedestrians inside the crossing. Simulations are run for as many steps as needed to cover the time interval covered by the experimental data.
